notes: Detailed assessment of trade union CCFA success fees; three points of principle are clearly resolved in the claimant's favour.

enrichment.short_title: CCFA success fees and client information in detailed assessment
key_facts: A firefighter's personal injury claim against Port Ramsgate settled for £130,000 plus costs after detailed assessment proceedings were transferred to the Supreme Court Costs Office.
Thompsons acted under a collective conditional fee agreement between the Fire Brigades Union and the firm, signed on 30 November 2000.

The defendant challenged recoverability of success fees and argued repudiatory breach of the CCFA, circularity under Customs & Excise v Vaz, and illegality of pre-agreement no-win-no-fee work inferred from retrospective terms.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Detailed assessment before a High Court costs judge on three preliminary points of principle affecting a trade union funded CCFA bill.
enrichment.outcome: All three points of principle decided in favour of the claimant; no repudiatory breach of information obligations, no Vaz circularity defect, and no inference of prior illegal no-win-no-fee terms.
enrichment.ratio: Under a valid CCFA with a trade union member, adequate explanation of the member's liability need not mirror full client-care disclosure given to privately funded litigants; charges calculated on allowable hourly rates are not limited to sums recovered from the opponent; and willingness to agree retrospective CCFA terms does not infer earlier unlawful conditional arrangements.
legal_issues: Whether failure to give detailed costs estimates under the CCFA amounted to repudiatory breach
Whether clause 4.3 of the CCFA offended the indemnity principle in Customs & Excise v Vaz
Whether retrospective CCFA coverage rendered pre-agreement profit costs irrecoverable as illegal no-win-no-fee work
linked_authorities: Hollins v Russell [2003] EWCA Civ 718
Customs & Excise Commissioners v Vaz [1995] STC 14
The Accident Group Test Cases Tranche 2 (15 May 2003, unreported)

confidence.notes: The three points of principle and outcomes are explicit. Some quantum and remaining assessment issues were reserved for a later hearing.

notes: Second appeal on ancillary relief charge triggers; limited variation by consent and on children leaving home is straightforward.

enrichment.short_title: Matrimonial home charge triggers on second ancillary relief appeal
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Sawden appeared in person on a renewed second appeal from ancillary relief orders giving the husband 45% and the wife 55% of equity in the former matrimonial home.
The charge on the wife's interest was enforceable on remarriage, cohabitation, sale, death, or six months' non-occupation, with a roll-over provision for one further home.
The husband, aged 58 and in ill health, argued he would never realise his share while the adult children Luke and Leah remained at home.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal and, if granted, appeal against ancillary relief orders under CPR 52.13 as a second appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in limited respects: surplus on a trade-down to be shared 45:45, and the charge to be realised when both children leave home and settle independently unless the wife buys the husband out; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where a second appeal is otherwise hard to justify on principle, a compelling reason exists if the existing order makes it a real likelihood that one spouse will never receive his equitable share; fairness may require an additional trigger when adult children leave home even where the wife has strong attachment to the property.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 52.13 permitted a second appeal on roll-over and surplus-capital points
Whether surplus on trading down should be shared with the husband
Whether the charge should crystallise when adult children leave the matrimonial home

confidence.notes: Outcome and varied triggers are clear. Detailed valuation figures were background only.

notes: Legitimate expectation and committal for sentence after cannabis cultivation pleas; unrecorded magistrates' proceedings noted but core reasoning is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Legitimate expectation not to be committed for sentence after magistrates accept jurisdiction
key_facts: Carl White faced either-way offences of large-scale cannabis cultivation and unlawful electricity abstraction at council flats in Barking and Devon.
On 8 August 2003 magistrates said they accepted jurisdiction and ordered a pre-sentence report with all sentencing options open including custody, without mentioning committal for sentence.
On 12 September 2003 a differently constituted bench committed him to Snaresbrook Crown Court for sentence despite no material change in the facts.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of a magistrates' court decision to commit the claimant for sentence after an earlier indication that magistrates would sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review refused; although a legitimate expectation was created, implementing it would require enforcement of a decision that would have been Wednesbury unreasonable and unlawful given the seriousness of the offences.
enrichment.ratio: Where magistrates indicate they will retain sentencing jurisdiction without expressly reserving committal for sentence, a legitimate expectation may arise; but judicial review will not enforce that expectation if retaining jurisdiction would have been a decision no reasonable bench could properly have made on the facts before it.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates' words on 8 August created a legitimate expectation of sentencing in the magistrates' court
Whether any misapprehension as to diseased cannabis plants vitiated that expectation
Whether the expectation should nevertheless be enforced despite later committal for sentence
linked_authorities: R v Davidson

confidence.notes: Legal analysis is detailed though based partly on reconstructed magistrates' proceedings without a transcript.

notes: Green Belt planning appeal quashed for PPG2 paragraph 3.4 error; inspector's sparse reasoning noted but quashing ground is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Green Belt all-weather riding yard planning appeal quashed
key_facts: Bravebyte Ltd sought retrospective planning permission for an all-weather outdoor exercise yard at the London Equestrian Centre in North Finchley within the Metropolitan Green Belt.
Grass surfacing authorised in 1998 proved inadequate for regular equestrian use with shod horses.
An inspector refused permission after treating the yard as inappropriate Green Belt development and finding no very special circumstances.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to the Secretary of State's decision dismissing a written-representation planning appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Application allowed; inspector's decision quashed with agreed costs of £6,800 including VAT payable by the Secretary of State.
enrichment.ratio: Misapplying PPG2 paragraph 3.4 to treat surfacing of an already permitted exercise area as inappropriate Green Belt development materially infected the inspector's very-special-circumstances analysis; visual-amenity harm alone engages a lower planning balance than inappropriate development requiring very special circumstances.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 3.4 of PPG2 was wrongly applied to non-building surfacing works
Whether the Green Belt error permeated the very-special-circumstances assessment
Whether refusal could stand independently on Area of Special Character harm alone

confidence.notes: Primary quashing reason is explicit. Secondary visual-comparison points are supportive rather than decisive alone.

notes: False imprisonment and malicious prosecution jury trial; judge-jury functions under Dallison are clearly stated.

enrichment.short_title: Speeding stop: jury should decide whether driver was exceeding limit
key_facts: Kensley Larrier was stopped on the M57/M62 after police recorded his VW Golf at a constant 95 mph in a 70 mph limit and detained him for about 45 minutes before issuing a ticket.
He was acquitted in the magistrates' court and then sued Merseyside Police for false imprisonment and malicious prosecution.
At trial the judge withdrew from the jury whether Larrier was in fact speeding and himself found reasonable cause to stop and prosecute.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against dismissal of false imprisonment and malicious prosecution claims after a county court judge ruled there was no jury issue on actual speed.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed with costs; October 2003 order set aside and claims remitted for retrial before a different judge and jury.
enrichment.ratio: Where police justification for stopping and prosecuting depends on a disputed factual account of speeding, the judge must leave the question whether the claimant was exceeding the speed limit to the jury before deciding reasonable cause; resolving that conflict himself was contrary to Dallison v Caffery and Balchin.
legal_issues: Whether the judge erred in deciding actual speed rather than leaving it to the jury
Whether reasonable cause to stop could be decided independently of the speed dispute
Whether police power under section 163 sufficed without a capricious-stop analysis
linked_authorities: Dallison v Caffery [1965] 1 QB 348
Balchin v Chief Constable of Hampshire Constabulary [2001] EWCA Civ 538
Gregory v Portsmouth City Council [2000] 1 AC 419

confidence.notes: Court of Appeal restates settled judge-jury principles and orders retrial without difficulty.

notes: Long section 287 local plan challenge over Old Sarum Airfield LSS boundary; both grounds dismissed with detailed reasoning.

enrichment.short_title: Old Sarum Airfield local plan landscape setting boundary upheld

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Development Plan) (England) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Blanefield Property Company challenged the 2003 Replacement Salisbury District Local Plan in respect of Old Sarum Airfield, which it leased from the MoD for 999 years.
The plan Inspector recommended deleting commercial buildings south of Portway from the Landscape Setting of Salisbury designation, but the Compass Maritime site remained within the LSS.
Blanefield also sought introduction of a late criteria-based airfield development policy after a quashed conservation area designation and refused section 78 appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 287 application to quash parts of an adopted replacement local plan relating to landscape setting boundaries and airfield policy.
enrichment.outcome: Challenge dismissed on both grounds; the council reasonably interpreted the Inspector's recommendation and adequately considered Blanefield's late policy proposal.
enrichment.ratio: A local planning authority may reasonably treat the Compass Maritime site as outside the Inspector's 'area of commercial buildings south of Portway' because it is largely open and undeveloped; failure to adopt a late criteria-based airfield policy did not prejudice the applicant where development had already been independently rejected by two inspectors and existing policies sufficed.
legal_issues: Whether retaining the Compass Maritime site within the LSS implemented the Inspector's recommendation
Whether the council gave adequate reasons for modifying the LSS boundary
Whether a material change after quashing the conservation area required a new airfield policy or further inquiry
linked_authorities: Warren v Uttlesford District Council [1997] JPL 1130
Save Britain's Heritage v Number 1 Poultry Ltd [1991] 1 WLR 153
Bellway Homes v West Berkshire Council [2003] EWHC 105

confidence.notes: Outcome and principal planning-law reasoning are clear in a very long judgment with extensive factual chronology.

notes: PACE admissibility of misspelling evidence at interview; Recorder's voir dire findings upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Admissibility of misspelling 'Jutin' evidence in criminal damage trial

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: The appellant was convicted of four counts of criminal damage after 83 cars at a St Austell garage were scratched with 'Fuck you Jutin'.
Justin Hawkins, son of the garage owner, had stopped payment on the appellant's wages cheque.
In police interview the appellant wrote 'Fuck you Jutin' twelve times and admitted spelling Justin as J-U-T-I-N; forensic comparison was impossible.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with leave against conviction after the trial judge rejected voir dire applications to exclude interview spelling evidence under PACE sections 76 and 78.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; spelling admission was admissible under section 76(4)(b) and not unfair under section 78.
enrichment.ratio: An oral admission in interview of how the accused spells a name may be used to show his mode of expression even where a wider confession is excluded; police need not disclose every piece of evidence pre-interview, and telling a suspect spelling 'does not matter' when seeking handwriting samples does not bar later reliance on the misspelling admitted.
legal_issues: Whether the spelling admission was a confession improperly obtained under section 76(2)
Whether section 76(4)(b) permitted use of the spelling evidence
Whether non-disclosure of the Jutin graffiti before interview rendered evidence unfair under section 78
linked_authorities: R v Voisin [1918] 1 KB 531
R v Roble [1997] Crim LR 449

confidence.notes: Appellate review of Recorder's voir dire findings is concise and conclusive.

notes: Asylum adjudicator quashed for confusing Somali and Kibajuni language evidence; expert-report reasoning flaws are explicit.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum appeal quashed after adjudicator confused Bajuni language evidence

statutes_considered.title: Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: The claimant claimed asylum as a Bajuni from Somalia who had fled civil war via Kenya.
The Secretary of State refused asylum mainly because she did not speak Kibajuni or Somali and lacked credible local knowledge.
Dr Virginia Luling's expert report, served without Home Office response, concluded after a Kibajuni interview that the claimant was a Bajuni from Somalia.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an immigration adjudicator's dismissal of Convention and ECHR appeals.
enrichment.outcome: Application allowed; adjudicator's decision quashed and the appeal remitted to a different adjudicator unless the Secretary of State changed his decision; claimant awarded costs.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator fatally erred by treating the claimant's limited Somali as proof she spoke very little Kibajuni, her diagnostic native dialect; rejection of Dr Luling's report without grappling with detailed geographic and cultural knowledge, after the Home Office failed to respond to an offer to call the expert, also rendered the decision unsafe.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator confused Somali and Kibajuni in assessing ethnicity
Whether Dr Luling's uncross-examined report was fairly discounted
Whether alternative safe-return findings were adequately reasoned
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex parte Khanafer [1996] Imm AR 212
Adan

confidence.notes: Moses J identifies specific reasoning flaws with unusual clarity; safe-return alternative analysis is secondary.

notes: Landlord and Tenant Act 1988 breach and exemplary damages after obstructive licence-to-assign process; very long fact-find but holdings are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Landlord's delay refusing licence to assign shop lease to Kelly Hoppen
key_facts: Design Progression Ltd sought licence to assign a substantially under-rented Fulham Road shop lease with two years remaining to interior designer Kelly Hoppen for a £75,000 premium.
Thurloe Properties' agents repeatedly demanded further financial information and costs despite strong references, accounts, and later a rent-deposit offer.
The landlord pursued a strategy to recover possession and re-let at market rent rather than consent to the assignment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for breach of statutory duty under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1988 for failure to respond within a reasonable time to an application for licence to assign, with damages and exemplary damages.
enrichment.outcome: Tenant succeeded; reasonable time expired by 21 March 2002 or alternatively 25 April 2002; compensatory and exemplary damages awarded including £25,000 exemplary damages; counterclaim dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Once a reasonable time to decide a licence-to-assign application expires without a decision, the landlord is in breach of section 1 of the 1988 Act and cannot later rely on fresh reasons; deliberate dilatory obstruction to frustrate an assignment and capture reversionary value may also attract exemplary damages under the second Rookes v Barnard limb.
legal_issues: When a reasonable time to respond to the assignment application expired
Whether failure to decide amounted to deemed unreasonable refusal under Go West
Whether the landlord's conduct justified exemplary damages
linked_authorities: Go West Ltd v Spigarolo [2003] QB 1140
Norwich Union Life Insurance Society v Shipmoor Ltd [1999] 1 WLR 531
Footwear Corporation Ltd v Amplight Properties Ltd [1999] 1 WLR 551
Rookes v Barnard [1964] AC 1129
Kuddus v Chief Constable of Leicester Constabulary [2002] 2 AC 122

confidence.notes: Liability holdings and exemplary award are explicit though damages figures involve some judicial adjustment.

notes: Permission-to-appeal decision on miscarriage-of-justice compensation under section 133; merits not finally decided.

enrichment.short_title: Permission to appeal miscarriage compensation deductions under section 133
key_facts: Michael and Vincent Hickey were convicted of Carl Bridgewater's murder in 1979 and spent long periods in custody before their convictions were quashed in 1997.
They and Michael O'Brien sought judicial review of compensation awards by Lord Brennan QC as Independent Assessor under section 133.
Maurice Kay J upheld deductions from non-pecuniary awards for other convictions and the assessor's approach to categorising damages.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed applications for permission to appeal Maurice Kay J's refusal of judicial review of Independent Assessor compensation decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted to the Hickeys on construction of section 133(4A), consistency of aggravated damages, and non-pecuniary awards; Independent Assessor's permission enlarged on breakdown and aggravated-compensation grounds.
enrichment.ratio: At permission stage, it is at least arguable that section 133(4A) deductions for 'similar damage' should not reduce awards attributable to official misconduct, loss of liberty, or aggravated damages; and that unexplained disparity between assessors' treatment of co-wrongly-convicted applicants may warrant appellate review in cases of this importance.
legal_issues: Construction of 'suffering, harm to reputation or similar damage' in section 133(4A)
Whether deductions may be made from misconduct, liberty, and aggravated-damage awards for unrelated convictions
Whether inconsistent aggravated and non-pecuniary awards between applicants breached equality principles
Whether the assessor was required to break down awards by Thompson v MPC categories
linked_authorities: Thompson v Metropolitan Police Commissioner [1998] QB 498

confidence.notes: This judgment grants permission only; substantive compensation principles remain for the full appeal.
